transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, thank you. Um… I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I’m noticing it more at work. I manage health services, and I’ll sit down to start an EPIC quality report or go into a clinic metrics meeting fully intending to pay attention, and then a few minutes later I realize my mind has really drifted.

It’s embarrassing, because I’ll be rereading the same numbers over and over, or I’ll realize I missed the main point of what someone was saying. I don’t want to overstate it—I’m still getting things done—but it’s happening enough that I thought I should probably talk to someone about it, if that makes sense.
Looking back, did you have these kinds of attention problems as a child?

Yes… I think so, although I always did okay in school, so I don’t know if anyone thought of it as a “problem” exactly.

Even in elementary school, I remember teachers saying I was bright but careless. And my mom had to sit with me to get homework finished sometimes, because I’d lose track of what I was supposed to do, or I’d forget a book at school. It feels a little silly saying that now, but looking back, yes, there were signs, I think.
When your mind drifts at work, is it usually because you’re worrying about something?

Not usually, no. I mean, I do have normal work stress, of course, but when this happens it doesn’t feel like I’m caught up worrying about something specific.

It’s more like… I sit down to do an EPIC quality report, or I’m in a clinic metrics meeting, and I really do intend to follow along. Then a few minutes later I realize I’ve drifted, and I’m rereading the same numbers or I’ve missed the point someone just made. It’s frustrating, because I’m trying to pay attention. Does that answer what you mean?
Do you notice the same kind of trouble paying attention in your home life, too?

I do, yes… though I’d say it’s the same kind of thing, just maybe less obvious than at work because there aren’t reports or meetings making it stand out.

At work, it’s really clear to me because I can start an EPIC quality report or sit in a clinic metrics meeting fully meaning to track it, and then within a few minutes my mind has gone somewhere else. Then I’m rereading the same numbers or realizing I missed the main point of what was being discussed.

So at home, I think it’s there too, but the work examples are the ones that made me feel like, okay, maybe I should actually ask about this. Does that make sense?
About how old were you when you first started noticing this kind of trouble paying attention?

Probably elementary school age… I don’t remember an exact year, but that’s when I first remember it showing up.

Teachers would write things like I was “bright but careless,” which at the time didn’t seem like a huge deal, maybe just me being a kid. And my mom sometimes had to sit with me while I finished homework because I’d lose track of what I was supposed to be doing, or I’d forget a book at school. So… I guess fairly young. Does that help?
Have these attention problems gotten noticeably worse only in the last few years?

I wouldn’t say it only started in the last few years… but it definitely became more noticeable then.

When I got promoted about two years and four months ago, my portfolio got a lot bigger, and the systems I’d always used to keep myself on track just didn’t seem to hold up as well. So it’s not like it came out of nowhere, but that’s when it started feeling harder to manage and harder to explain away. Does that fit with what you’re asking?
Have these attention problems ever caused a significant problem for you at work, school, or at home?

Yes… I think it has, although I don’t want to overstate it.

At work, the delays have started to matter more. Some of my clinic reporting deadlines have slipped, and then that means other teams are waiting on me, which feels awful because I really don’t want to be the bottleneck.

And outside of work, I’ve had to step back from leading parts of the volunteer health workshops I help with, because I just couldn’t reliably keep all the planning pieces moving the way I should. I can still contribute, but being the person responsible for coordinating it was getting… not fair to everyone else, I guess.

So yes, I’d say it’s caused problems. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Are you having trouble with your memory, like forgetting recent conversations or appointments?

Not so much like I completely forget whole conversations, I don’t think… but there are moments that are embarrassing.

Like if a medical director or one of my coordinators is talking directly to me, I’ll be looking at them, nodding, seeming like I’m following, and then a minute later I realize the action item didn’t really stick. I’ll have to ask them to repeat what they need from me.

I try to play it off as wanting to be clear, but it does happen. Does that count as memory trouble, or is that more attention?
Do you often feel restless or fidgety?

Not really, no… at least not in a way I’ve thought of as a problem.

I might shift in my chair or tap a pen sometimes, but I wouldn’t say I feel driven to move around or anything like that. I’m not sure if there’s a specific kind of restlessness you mean, though.
Have you been feeling down or depressed বেশ a lot lately?

I don’t think so… not “depressed” in the way I understand it.

I get frustrated with myself, and sometimes I feel pretty discouraged when I’m behind or I’ve let something slip, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been feeling down most of the time. At least, I haven’t really thought of it that way.

Is that the distinction you’re asking about?
Do you often feel anxious or on edge?

I wouldn’t say often, no. I mean, I get tense when I know I’m behind or when something is hanging over me, but I don’t feel like I’m anxious or on edge all the time.

Maybe I’m just used to operating with a certain level of stress at work, so I don’t always notice it. But I don’t think anxiety is the main thing, if that makes sense.
Do you often forget recent conversations even when you were paying attention at the time?

Sometimes, yes… though I feel a little embarrassed saying that because I am trying to listen.

Like if a medical director or one of my coordinators is talking right to me, I’ll be looking at them and nodding, and I really do think I’m paying attention. But then when it gets to the action item, I sometimes have to ask them to repeat it because it just… didn’t stick. The words don’t stay with me the way they should.

I try to cover it by taking notes, but yes, that does happen.
Have you had trouble finding common words in conversation?

Not really, no. I mean, I’ll occasionally lose a word like anyone does, especially if I’m tired, but I haven’t noticed that being a particular problem for me.

If anything, I might pause to make sure I’m saying things clearly, but I don’t think I’m often struggling to find common words. Does that answer what you mean?
Have you gotten lost in places that should be familiar to you?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I might take a wrong turn in a parking garage or somewhere unfamiliar, but in places I know, I don’t really get lost.

At least, not in a way that’s stood out to me as a problem. Is that what you mean?
Have other people started noticing that your memory is getting worse?

I don’t think so, not in a major way. I mean, people might remind me of things here and there, but no one has sat me down or said they’re worried that my memory is getting worse.

At least, if they have noticed, they haven’t said it to me directly. Does that make sense?
When you write the action item down right away, are you usually able to remember it later?

Usually if I write it down, that helps, yes. But I guess… it doesn’t always mean I actually circle back to it.

Like after a committee meeting, if someone gives me three or four follow-up things, I’ll jot them down and I may do the first one, maybe even start the second. But then something like the email or spreadsheet or final submission can just sort of sit there unfinished until someone reminds me. I’m not trying to ignore it—it’s more like I lose the thread unless it gets brought back to my attention. Does that make sense?
Do you often start tasks but have trouble finishing them?

Yes… I think that does happen. I don’t want to make it sound like I never finish anything, because I do, but with multi-step things I can lose momentum.

Like after a committee meeting, if someone gives me three or four follow-up items, I’ll usually do the first one, and maybe I’ll start drafting the second. But then the email, or spreadsheet, or whatever final submission is needed can just sit there unfinished until someone reminds me. It’s not intentional—I just sort of lose track of the end of it. Does that answer what you’re asking?
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or keeping track of the steps in a project?

Yes, I think so… though I don’t want to overstate it. It’s not like I can’t organize anything at all.

But if there are several steps, especially after a committee meeting, I can lose track of the sequence. Someone might give me three or four follow-up items, and I’ll do the first one, maybe draft the second, and then the email or spreadsheet or final submission just kind of sits there. I may not realize it’s still unfinished until someone reminds me.

So yes, keeping track of all the steps is probably harder for me than it should be. Does that make sense?
Compared with a few years ago, do you feel your memory is clearly getting worse?

I don’t think I’d say it’s clearly getting worse, no. At least, not in a way that feels like a major change from a few years ago.

I’ve always had to write things down and use reminders, so sometimes it’s hard for me to tell what’s “memory” versus just… my usual way of keeping track of things. But I haven’t noticed a big decline, if that’s what you mean. Does that answer it?
